Well, hi, doctor. Thanks for seeing me. I, uh, I guess what brings me in is... well, it’s this feeling I get. It's hard to explain, but it’s like I’ve got this, this motor just humming right under my skin. Especially whenever I’m supposed to just sit still, you know? 

Like, at work—I'm a building cleaner, mostly doing maintenance and janitorial stuff—and we have these staff meetings every Tuesday morning. They aren't even that long, maybe forty-five minutes, but I just... I can't do it. I'm sitting there in those cheap plastic chairs and my legs are practically vibrating. Or, like, at my church. I help out with the event briefings, setting up the fellowship hall and going over the schedule with the committee, and they all just sit around this big oak table talking and talking. And I try, I really try to just stay put and listen, but that humming feeling gets so intense I end up shifting my weight constantly, crossing and uncrossing my legs, or I just flat out stand up in the middle of someone talking. 

I always have to find some excuse to move around. I'll say something like, 'Oh, let me go check the thermostat,' or 'I'll go grab us some more coffee from the kitchen,' even if nobody actually wants any coffee. It's just... I don't know, it's driving me a little crazy because I'm 56 years old, I feel like I should be able to sit through a simple briefing without feeling like I'm gonna explode out of my chair. But I just can't seem to stop moving once that motor starts going, and people are starting to look at me funny when I'm pacing around the back of the room.

Well, um... act on impulse? Like, doing things without thinking? No, I... I really don't think so. I mean, sure, I might pop out of my chair in the middle of a meeting like I was just telling you, but that’s not me making some kind of rash decision or anything, that’s just my body needing to move. But as far as actually making choices or doing things without thinking them through? No, I'm actually pretty methodical. 

Take my supply cart, for example. When I get to the maintenance closet at the start of my shift, I don't just start grabbing bottles of glass cleaner and paper towel rolls willy-nilly. I stop, I look at my route for the night, and I think about exactly what I'm going to need. I know that the third floor goes through paper towels twice as fast as the first floor because of the big breakroom up there, so I plan for that. I think it all out. 

And it’s the same way at home, or with my money, or, you know, making big decisions. I don't just go out and buy a new shop vac or a floor buffer without reading up on it first, checking the specs, comparing the prices at a few different hardware stores. I mean, I’ve got my associate's degree, I learned a long time ago how to do my research and plan things out before I make a move. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive at all. If anything, I might overthink things sometimes, just making sure I’ve got all my ducks in a row before I start my shift or take on a new project at the church. Because if you don't plan ahead in this line of work, you end up halfway down a long hallway with a mop and no ringer bucket, and then you're just wasting time walking all the way back. So yeah, I definitely think things through. I don't just jump into things blind.

Fidgeting with my hands or feet? Hmm. No, I wouldn't really say that. I know I mentioned earlier that my legs get that vibrating feeling, but that's more of an internal pressure, like a whole-body urge to just stand up and get moving. It's not like I'm sitting there tapping my toes to some imaginary beat or twiddling my thumbs. 

My hands are actually pretty still. Mostly because, well, after a long shift of gripping a mop handle or wringing out those heavy industrial sponges, my hands are just plain tired. I usually just rest them flat on my lap, or maybe I'll hold onto my coffee mug. Like at the church briefings, I always have this big ceramic mug—my wife got it for me a few years back, it's got a picture of a golden retriever on it since we used to have one back in the nineties—and I just hold it with both hands. I'm not drumming my fingers on the table or picking at my fingernails or peeling the label off a water bottle like you see some folks doing when they get bored in a meeting. I just hold the mug. 

And my feet, they're usually just planted flat on the floor. I wear these heavy steel-toed Red Wing boots to work—great for arch support, by the way, which you absolutely need when you're walking on concrete floors all night, otherwise your lower back is just shot by Thursday—and they're so heavy I'm not really bouncing my feet around in them or wiggling my ankles. 

So no, I'm not really a toe-tapper or a finger-drummer. The feeling I get, that motor I was talking about, it's just this overwhelming need to get up and walk around, to actually be on the move, rather than just playing with my hands or bouncing a foot. If I'm sitting, my hands and feet are pretty quiet, it's just the rest of me that feels like it's going to jump out of my skin if I don't find a reason to go check the hallway.

Sitting still as a kid? Oh, boy... yeah. Yeah, absolutely. I remember getting in a whole lot of trouble back in grade school for exactly that. It wasn't that I was a bad kid, you know, I wasn't malicious or picking fights on the playground or anything like that, but I just could not stay in that little wooden chair. I'd be popping out of my seat right in the middle of a lesson—just standing up to go check the pencil sharpener or look out the window, just like I do now in those staff meetings I was telling you about. 

And it wasn't just the standing up, either. I was always talking right over the teacher. Mrs. Higgins, I think her name was, third grade... I'd just blurt things out while she was still talking. Or she'd be handing out a spelling worksheet, and I'd be rushing ahead, grabbing my pencil and trying to fill out the answers before she was even finished giving the directions. I’d end up doing half of it wrong just because I couldn't wait for her to get to the end of her sentence. I just had to go, go, go. 

My mother, God rest her soul, she used to say it all the time. She’d look at me running circles around the living room and she'd say I acted like I was wound too tight. Even as a little kid. She used to compare me to one of those little tin wind-up toys, where you turn the key in the back too many times and it just skitters all over the kitchen linoleum until it hits the baseboards. "He's wound too tight," she’d tell my dad when he got home from the plant. Trying to get me to just sit at the dinner table for ten minutes to eat a plate of meatloaf without me jumping up to check on the dog or see what was happening out in the yard was like trying to nail Jell-O to the wall. So, yeah, it's definitely not a new thing for me. It’s been happening since I was in short pants.

Diagnosed? No. No, never anything official like that. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Lose track? Forget what I'm doing? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, my memory for my zones and my tasks is sharp as a tack. It's really just the sitting still and the waiting around that gets me, not the actual doing of the work. 

When I have a job in front of me, I know exactly what needs to be done. Take my supply cart, for instance. Every single shift, before I even hit the floor, I have a very specific way I stock that cart. I've got the glass cleaner on the left, the heavy-duty degreaser on the right, extra trash liners—both the clear ones for the little office bins and the heavy black ones for the main breakroom—tucked right underneath the main tray. And I never, ever forget to check the stock on the C-fold paper towels or the foam soap refills before I head out. I mean, you can ask anyone on the crew. Even Dave, as much as he gets on my case about rushing and being impatient, he can't ever say I forgot to do a task or left a job half-finished because I lost my train of thought. 

If anything, I finish the tasks too quickly because I'm just blasting right through them. Like when I'm doing the third-floor restrooms, I am in and out. I hit the mirrors, scrub the sinks, swap the bins, mop the tile, and I'm already onto the next zone before the other guys have even finished putting up the wet floor signs in the hallway. I don't walk into a room and stand there scratching my head wondering why I went in there, you know? My brain doesn't just drop the ball like that. 

Susan will tell you the exact same thing at home. If she gives me a list for the hardware store, I don't forget what I went in for. I get the weatherstripping, I get the wood glue, I get the exact right size screws. I just might pace up and down the aisles and tap my foot out of my mind if the guy in front of me at the checkout is taking too long counting his loose change. So, no, losing track of things or forgetting what I'm supposed to be doing, that really isn't an issue for me. It's just the speed I'm doing it at, and how much it physically bothers me to slow down.

Then I move right on to the restrooms, checking the soap dispensers, wiping down the mirrors, mopping the tile. I follow through on every bit of it. I don't just wander off and leave a mop bucket sitting in the middle of the hallway, you know? I finish what I start. \n\nEven at home, or over at the church, if I say I'm gonna set up the folding chairs, I'm out there doing it until every last chair is perfectly lined up. So, no, my mind doesn't wander off into the clouds or anything like that. It's not a focus thing. I know exactly what I'm supposed to be doing and I get it done. If anything, I probably pay more attention to the details than half the younger guys they hire these days, mostly because I'm always on my feet, always moving around and checking things anyway. So no, finishing tasks isn't the problem at all. It's just the sitting still part.\n\nDoctor: Do you often act on impulse without thinking things through?\n\nPatient: Well, um... act on impulse? But as far as actually making choices or doing things without thinking them through? No, I'm actually pretty methodical. \n\nTake my supply cart, for example. When I get to the maintenance closet at the start of my shift, I don't just start grabbing bottles of glass cleaner and paper towel rolls willy-nilly. I think it all out. \n\nAnd it’s the same way at home, or with my money, or, you know, making big decisions. I don't just go out and buy a new shop vac or a floor buffer without reading up on it first, checking the specs, comparing the prices at a few different hardware stores. I mean, I’ve got my associate's degree, I learned a long time ago how to do my research and plan things out before I make a move. \n\nSo, no, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive at all. I don't just jump into things blind.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself fidgeting with your hands or feet when you're sitting still?\n\nPatient: Fidgeting with my hands or feet? Hmm. Well, socially? With family? I mean, Susan just gets annoyed when I pace during her shows, like I was saying, but we've been married twenty-eight years, so she's used to it by now. Oh, it's the urge. Definitely the urge. It’s not about my focus at all. Like I was saying before about my memory being sharp, my brain is right there, it’s just my body that won't cooperate. It starts as a foot tap, then my knee is bouncing, and I end up shifting all my weight from one side to the other, leaning back, leaning forward, just trying to relieve the pressure in my muscles.

And I'm sitting there in the folding chair, and that same humming feeling just takes over. I can't take it. I end up having to stand up and pace in the back of the room, or I'll just find some excuse to move around. I'll suddenly blurt out, "Hey, I'm gonna go check if the coffee urns are plugged in," and I'll literally go check coffee pots that I know for a fact I haven't even filled with water yet, just so I can walk down the corridor. Because if I don't get up and move, if I try to just sit there and ignore that motor, I feel like I'm gonna crawl right out of my own skin. So, yeah, it's 100 percent a physical need to be active, not my brain losing focus.

Well, it's... it's a bit of both, honestly, but I'd say the real problem, the thing that really gets under my skin and makes me want to snap, is the waiting. The waiting is just agonizing. Even Dave, as much as he gets on my case about rushing and being impatient, he can't ever say I forgot to do a task or left a job half-finished because I lost my train of thought. \n\nIf anything, I finish the tasks too quickly because I'm just blasting right through them. Like when I'm doing the third-floor restrooms, I am in and out. I hit the mirrors, scrub the sinks, swap the bins, mop the tile, and I'm already onto the next zone before the other guys have even finished putting up the wet floor signs in the hallway. I don't walk into a room and stand there scratching my head wondering why I went in there, you know? My brain doesn't just drop the ball like that. \n\nSusan will tell you the exact same thing at home. If she gives me a list for the hardware store, I don't forget what I went in for. I get the weatherstripping, I get the wood glue, I get the exact right size screws. So, no, losing track of things or forgetting what I'm supposed to be doing, that really isn't an issue for me. It's just the speed I'm doing it at, and how much it physically bothers me to slow down.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulty with sitting still and the humming feeling have caused significant problems in your social relationships, such as with friends or family members?\n\nPatient: Well, socially? Never even thought to ask for one until this whole mess with the rotating shifts started up and pushed me to the point where I'm sitting in an office like this.\n\nDoctor: Do you often struggle to complete tasks because you lose track of what you're doing or forget what you need to do?\n\nPatient: Lose track? Forget what I'm doing? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, my memory for my zones and my tasks is sharp as a tack. It's really just the sitting still and the waiting around that gets me, not the actual doing of the work. \n\nWhen I have a job in front of me, I know exactly what needs to be done. Take my supply cart, for instance. Every single shift, before I even hit the floor, I have a very specific way I stock that cart. I've got the glass cleaner on the left, the heavy-duty degreaser on the right, extra trash liners—both the clear ones for the little office bins and the heavy black ones for the main breakroom—tucked right underneath the main tray. And I never, ever forget to check the stock on the C-fold paper towels or the foam soap refills before I head out. I mean, you can ask anyone on the crew. Even Dave, as much as he gets on my case about rushing and being impatient, he can't ever say I forgot to do a task or left a job half-finished because I lost my train of thought. \n\nIf anything, I finish the tasks too quickly because I'm just blasting right through them. Like when I'm doing the third-floor restrooms, I am in and out. I hit the mirrors, scrub the sinks, swap the bins, mop the tile, and I'm already onto the next zone before the other guys have even finished putting up the wet floor signs in the hallway. I don't walk into a room and stand there scratching my head wondering why I went in there, you know? My brain doesn't just drop the ball like that. \n\nSusan will tell you the exact same thing at home. If she gives me a list for the hardware store, I don't forget what I went in for. I get the weatherstripping, I get the wood glue, I get the exact right size screws. I just might pace up and down the aisles and tap my foot out of my mind if the guy in front of me at the checkout is taking too long counting his loose change. So, no, losing track of things or forgetting what I'm supposed to be doing, that really isn't an issue for me. It's just the speed I'm doing it at, and how much it physically bothers me to slow down.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulty with sitting still and the humming feeling have caused significant problems in your social relationships, such as with friends or family members?\n\nPatient: Well, socially? With family? I mean, Susan just gets annoyed when I pace during her shows, like I was saying, but we've been married twenty-eight years, so she's used to it by now. She just points toward the garage and tells me to go find a project. And my buddies, they just know I'm the guy who's going to get up and pace or go grab the next round of drinks. So socially, no, it hasn't blown up my life or anything like that. \n\nBut... well, where it *is* causing a real, significant problem right now is at work. That's the whole reason I'm sitting here talking to you. It's started causing a lot of complaints from the other guys, and Dave is constantly pulling me in for corrections lately. Because with this humming feeling, this constant need to just *go* and get moving, I end up missing parts of the instructions. Like, Dave will be doing the pre-shift huddle, explaining what we need for a big event setup, and my legs are just bouncing under the table. I'll hear the first half of what he says—like, \"set up the main hall\"—and my brain is already halfway down the corridor. I'm out the door before he finishes telling us we need the round banquet tables instead of the long rectangular ones. So, it's not that I'm forgetting my routine, it's that I'm moving too fast to catch the whole instruction in the first place because I just can't sit there and listen to him drone on.\n\nAnd then, man, it creates all this friction with the rest of the crew. I'm in there, buzzing around, stacking chairs, breaking down stages, and the other guys—who, honestly, move like molasses in January—they get really frustrated with me. I'm stepping on their toes, or I'm rushing the supply decisions. We'll be standing at the utility closet, and they want to stand around debating which floor wax to use or how many boxes of liners to bring up, and I just physically cannot stand there and wait. It makes my skin crawl to just stand around debating. So I just grab the standard supplies and take off. \n\nAnd then, of course, they complain to Dave that I'm impossible to work with, that I'm bulldozing them and not working as a team. The friction is just getting really bad. It got to the point where Dave finally called me in, shut the door, and told me I was causing too many headaches with the crew and messing up too many event details. That's exactly when he pushed that Employee Assistance Program pamphlet across his desk at me. He basically said if I didn't get this restless motor of mine sorted out, it was going to be a real problem for my job. So, yeah, it's definitely causing issues, just mostly on the clock.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your difficulties with sitting still are more related to not being able to focus or more related to an internal urge to be active?\n\nPatient: Oh, it's the urge. Definitely the urge. It’s not about my focus at all. Like I was saying before about my memory being sharp, my brain is right there, it’s just my body that won't cooperate. Absent? No, doc, never. Not once in my entire fifty-six years on this earth. I mean, if I really try to rack my brain and think of a time where I was just... still? Where that motor was actually shut down? It just doesn't exist. It’s been this way my whole life. 

Even way back, I'm talking grade school... I remember getting in so much trouble back then. It was always the same story, year after year, whether it was Mrs. Gable in third grade or Mr. Henderson in fourth. I'd be constantly popping out of my seat. You know those little wooden desks with the attached chairs they used to have? I just couldn't stay glued to them. I'd be up sharpening my pencil for the fifth time, or walking over to the trash can, or I'd just be standing up beside my desk for no earthly reason other than my legs felt like they were vibrating and I had to stretch them. 

And the talking! Oh, I would just talk right over the teacher. They'd be in the middle of explaining a history lesson or long division, and I'd just blurt something out before they even finished their sentence. I was always rushing ahead before the directions were finished, too. Like, they'd hand out a mimeographed worksheet—you remember those old ones, with the purple ink that smelled sweet?—and the teacher would say, 'Now, everyone put your pencils down and wait until I tell you to start.' But I just couldn't wait. I’d already be halfway through the page before they even finished explaining what we were supposed to be doing, and half the time I’d do it completely wrong because I didn't actually listen to the instructions. I just had to get moving on it.

My mother, God rest her soul, she knew it too. She used to say I acted like I was wound too tight. That was her exact phrase, "wound too tight," even as a little kid. She’d be trying to get me to just sit at the kitchen table to eat a bologna sandwich, and I’d be eating it standing up, shifting from foot to foot, and she’d just sigh, shake her head, and tell me I was wound too tight. So, no, there's never been a period where this feeling was absent. It’s just... it's just always been there, running in the background, making me go, go, go.

Well, yeah, like I was just saying a minute ago, it definitely didn't start later in life. It was right there from the get-go. 

I remember getting in so much trouble back in grade school for exactly that kind of thing. I was always popping out of my seat when I was supposed to be sitting quietly. It was like a physical impossibility for me to just stay put in those little wooden chairs. And I'd just talk right over the teacher, blurting things out before they could even finish a thought. Plus, I was always rushing ahead before the directions were finished. And like I mentioned about my mother, she saw it too, right from the start. She used to say I acted like I was "wound too tight," even as a little kid. That was just her phrase for it. She'd be trying to get me to just sit down and eat, or just watch a television show, and I'd be practically vibrating, shifting from foot to foot. So, no, it definitely didn't develop when I got older or started working. It's been this exact same restlessness, this exact same inability to just stay put, since I was in short pants. It’s a wonder my teachers didn't pull all their hair out, honestly, because I just couldn't turn that motor off back then either.

Details? Careless mistakes? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, honestly, it's kind of the opposite, at least with the things I do every day. You'd think with me always rushing around, always having that motor going and needing to be moving, that I'd get sloppy, but I really don't.
